## Regular Expressions 

For information on regular expression syntax, see your data source's documentation. For Tableau extracts, regular expression syntax conforms to the standards of the ICU (International Components for Unicode), an open source project of mature C/C++ and Java libraries for Unicode support, software internationalization, and software globalization. See the [Regular Expressions](http://userguide.icu-project.org/strings/regexp) page in the online ICU User Guide.

### REGEXP\_REPLACE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;"><colgroup><col style="width: 20%;"><col></colgroup><tbody><tr><td>Syntax</td><td><code>REGEXP_REPLACE(string, pattern, replacement)</code></td></tr><tr><td>Output</td><td>String</td></tr><tr><td>Definition</td><td>Returns a copy of the given string where the regular expression pattern is replaced by the replacement string. </td></tr><tr><td>Example</td><td><pre>REGEXP_REPLACE('abc 123', '\s', '-') = 'abc-123'</pre></td></tr><tr><td>Notes</td><td><p>This function is available for Text File, Hadoop Hive, Google BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Tableau Data Extract, Microsoft Excel, Salesforce, Vertica, Pivotal Greenplum, Teradata (version 14.1 and above), Snowflake, and Oracle data sources. </p><p>For Tableau data extracts, the pattern and the replacement must be constants. </p></td></tr></tbody></table>

### REGEXP\_MATCH

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;"><colgroup><col style="width: 20%;"><col></colgroup><tbody><tr><td>Syntax</td><td><code>REGEXP_MATCH(string, pattern)</code></td></tr><tr><td>Output</td><td>Boolean</td></tr><tr><td>Definition</td><td>Returns true if a substring of the specified string matches the regular expression pattern.</td></tr><tr><td>Example</td><td><pre>REGEXP_MATCH('-([1234].[The.Market])-','\[\s*(\w*\.)(\w*\s*\])')=true</pre></td></tr><tr><td>Notes</td><td><p> This function is available for Text File, Google BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Tableau Data Extract, Microsoft Excel, Salesforce, Vertica, Pivotal Greenplum, Teradata (version 14.1 and above), Impala 2.3.0 (through Cloudera Hadoop data sources), Snowflake, and Oracle data sources. </p><p>For Tableau data extracts, the pattern must be a constant. </p></td></tr></tbody></table>

### REGEXP\_EXTRACT

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;"><colgroup><col style="width: 20%;"><col></colgroup><tbody><tr><td>Syntax</td><td><code>REGEXP_EXTRACT(string, pattern)</code></td></tr><tr><td>Output</td><td>String</td></tr><tr><td>Definition</td><td>Returns the portion of the string that matches the regular expression pattern. </td></tr><tr><td>Example</td><td><pre>REGEXP_EXTRACT('abc 123', '[a-z]+\s+(\d+)') = '123'</pre></td></tr><tr><td>Notes</td><td><p> This function is available for Text File, Hadoop Hive, Google BigQuery, PostgreSQL, Tableau Data Extract, Microsoft Excel, Salesforce, Vertica, Pivotal Greenplum, Teradata (version 14.1 and above), Snowflake, and Oracle data sources. </p><p>For Tableau data extracts, the pattern must be a constant. </p></td></tr></tbody></table>

### REGEXP\_EXTRACT\_NTH

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;"><colgroup><col style="width: 20%;"><col></colgroup><tbody><tr><td>Syntax</td><td><code>REGEXP_EXTRACT_NTH(string, pattern, index)</code></td></tr><tr><td>Output</td><td>String</td></tr><tr><td>Definition</td><td>Returns the portion of the string that matches the regular expression pattern. The substring is matched to the nth capturing group, where n is the given index. If index is 0, the entire string is returned. </td></tr><tr><td>Example</td><td><pre>REGEXP_EXTRACT_NTH('abc 123', '([a-z]+)\s+(\d+)', 2) = '123'</pre></td></tr><tr><td>Notes</td><td><p>This function is available for Text File, PostgreSQL, Tableau Data Extract, Microsoft Excel, Salesforce, Vertica, Pivotal Greenplum, Teradata (version 14.1 and above), and Oracle data sources.</p><p>For Tableau data extracts, the pattern must be a constant. </p></td></tr></tbody></table>

## Hadoop Hive Specific Functions

**Note**: Only the PARSE\_URL and PARSE\_URL\_QUERY functions are available for Cloudera Impala data sources.

### GET\_JSON\_OBJECT(JSON string, JSON path)

Returns the JSON object within the JSON string based on the JSON path.

### PARSE\_URL(string, url\_part)

Returns a component of the given URL string where the component is defined by url\_part. Valid url\_part values include: 'HOST', 'PATH', 'QUERY', 'REF', 'PROTOCOL', 'AUTHORITY', 'FILE' and 'USERINFO'.

Example

`PARSE_URL('http://www.tableau.com', 'HOST') = 'www.tableau.com'`

### PARSE\_URL\_QUERY(string, key)

Returns the value of the specified query parameter in the given URL string. The query parameter is defined by the key.

Example

`PARSE_URL_QUERY('http://www.tableau.com?page=1&cat=4', 'page') = '1'`

### XPATH\_BOOLEAN(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns true if the XPath expression matches a node or evaluates to true.

Example

`XPATH_BOOLEAN('<values> <value id="0">1</value><value id="1">5</value>', 'values/value[@id="1"] = 5') = true`

### XPATH\_DOUBLE(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the floating-point value of the XPath expression.

Example

`XPATH_DOUBLE('<values><value>1.0</value><value>5.5</value> </values>', 'sum(value/*)') = 6.5`

### XPATH\_FLOAT(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the floating-point value of the XPath expression.

Example

`XPATH_FLOAT('<values><value>1.0</value><value>5.5</value> </values>','sum(value/*)') = 6.5`

### XPATH\_INT(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the numerical value of the XPath expression, or zero if the XPath expression cannot evaluate to a number.

Example

`XPATH_INT('<values><value>1</value><value>5</value> </values>','sum(value/*)') = 6`

### XPATH\_LONG(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the numerical value of the XPath expression, or zero if the XPath expression cannot evaluate to a number.

Example

`XPATH_LONG('<values><value>1</value><value>5</value> </values>','sum(value/*)') = 6`

### XPATH\_SHORT(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the numerical value of the XPath expression, or zero if the XPath expression cannot evaluate to a number.

Example

`XPATH_SHORT('<values><value>1</value><value>5</value> </values>','sum(value/*)') = 6`

### XPATH\_STRING(XML string, XPath expression string)

Returns the text of the first matching node.

Example

`XPATH_STRING('<sites ><url domain="org">http://www.w3.org</url> <url domain="com">http://www.tableau.com</url></sites>', 'sites/url[@domain="com"]') = 'http://www.tableau.com'`

## Google BigQuery Specific Functions

### DOMAIN(string\_url)

Given a URL string, returns the domain as a string.

Example

`DOMAIN('http://www.google.com:80/index.html') = 'google.com'`

### GROUP\_CONCAT(expression)

Concatenates values from each record into a single comma-delimited string. This function acts like a SUM() for strings.

Example

`GROUP_CONCAT(Region) = "Central,East,West"`

### HOST(string\_url)

Given a URL string, returns the host name as a string.

Example

`HOST('http://www.google.com:80/index.html') = 'www.google.com:80'`

### LOG2(number)

Returns the logarithm base 2 of a number.

Example

`LOG2(16) = '4.00'`

### LTRIM\_THIS(string, string)

Returns the first string with any leading occurrence of the second string removed.

Example

`LTRIM_THIS('[-Sales-]','[-') = 'Sales-]'`

### RTRIM\_THIS(string, string)

Returns the first string with any trailing occurrence of the second string removed.

Example

`RTRIM_THIS('[-Market-]','-]') = '[-Market'`

### TIMESTAMP\_TO\_USEC(expression)

Converts a TIMESTAMP data type to a UNIX timestamp in microseconds.

Example

`TIMESTAMP_TO_USEC(#2012-10-01 01:02:03#)=1349053323000000`

### USEC\_TO\_TIMESTAMP(expression)

Converts a UNIX timestamp in microsseconds to a TIMESTAMP data type.

Example

`USEC_TO_TIMESTAMP(1349053323000000) = #2012-10-01 01:02:03#`

### TLD(string\_url)

Given a URL string, returns the top level domain plus any country domain in the URL.

Example

`TLD('http://www.google.com:80/index.html') = '.com'`

`TLD('http://www.google.co.uk:80/index.html') = '.co.uk'`

# Aggregate Functions in Tableau

This article introduces aggregate functions and their uses in Tableau. It also demonstrates how to create an aggregate calculation using an example.

## Why use aggregate functions

Aggregate functions allow you to summarize or change the granularity of your data.

For example, you might want to know exactly how many orders your store had for a particular year. You can use the COUNTD function to tally the exact number of unique orders your company had, and then break the visualization down by year.

The calculation might look something like this:

`COUNTD(Order ID)`

The visualization might look something like this:

![](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/aggregate_function1.png)

## Aggregate functions available in Tableau

**Aggregations and floating-point arithmetic**: The results of some aggregations may not always be exactly as expected. For example, you may find that the SUM function returns a value such as -1.42e-14 for a column of numbers that you know should sum to exactly 0. This happens because the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 754 floating-point standard requires that numbers be stored in binary format, which means that numbers are sometimes rounded at extremely fine levels of precision. You can eliminate this potential distraction by using the ROUND function (see [Number Functions](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_number.htm)) or by formatting the number to show fewer decimal places.

### ATTR

Otherwise returns an asterisk. Null values are ignored.</td></tr></tbody></table>

### AVG

### COUNT

### COVAR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>COVAR(expression1, expression2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the <i>sample</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Sample covariance</i> uses the number of non-null data points n - 1 to normalize the covariance calculation, rather than n, which is used by the population covariance (available with the <code>COVARP</code> function). Sample covariance is the appropriate choice when the data is a random sample that is being used to estimate the covariance for a larger population.</p>
                                <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVAR([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVAR</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed.</p>
                                <p>The value of <code>COVAR(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VAR(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEV(X)^2</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>COVAR</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica.</p>
                                <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### COVARP

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>COVARP(expression 1, expression2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the <i>population</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Population covariance</i> is sample covariance multiplied by (n-1)/n, where n is the total number of non-null data points. Population covariance is the appropriate choice when there is data available for all items of interest as opposed to when there is only a random subset of items, in which case sample covariance (with the <code>COVAR</code> function) is appropriate.
</p>
                                <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVARP([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVARP</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed.

Note: The value of <code>COVARP(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VARP(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEVP(X)^2</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>COVARP</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica</p>
                                <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><b>For strings</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                <p><b>For dates</b>
                                </p>
                                <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

                                <p>For other data source types, you can extract your data into an extract file to use this function. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/extracting_data.htm" target="_blank">Extract Your Data</a>.</p>

## Create an aggregate calculation

Follow along with the steps below to learn how to create an aggregate calculation.

1. In Tableau Desktop, connect to the **Sample - Superstore** saved data source, which comes with Tableau.
2. Navigate to a worksheet and select Analysis \> Create Calculated Field.
3. In the calculation editor that opens, do the following:
    
    - Name the calculated field Margin.
    - Enter the following formula:
        
        `IIF(SUM([Sales]) !=0, SUM([Profit])/SUM([Sales]), 0)`
        
        **Note**: You can use the function reference to find and add aggregate functions and other functions (like the logical IIF function in this example) to the calculation formula. For more information, see [Use the functions reference in the calculation editor](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_calculatedfields_tips.htm#functions).
    - When finished, click OK.
    
    The new aggregate calculation appears under **Measures** in the **Data** pane. Just like your other fields, you can use it in one or more visualizations.
    
    **Note**: Aggregation calculations are always measures.
    
    When Margin is placed on a shelf or card in the worksheet, its name is changed to AGG(Margin), which indicates that it is an aggregate calculation and cannot be aggregated any further.
    
    ![A graphic depicting what happens when you place an aggregate
    calculation on a shelf. The field displays the AGG prefix.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/calc_agg8.png)

## Rules for aggregate calculations

The rules that apply to aggregate calculations are as follows:

- For any aggregate calculation, you cannot combine an aggregated value and a disaggregated value. For example, `SUM(Price)*[Items]` is not a valid expression because SUM(Price) is aggregated and Items is not. However, `SUM(Price*Items)` and `SUM(Price)*SUM(Items)` are both valid.
- Constant terms in an expression act as aggregated or disaggregated values as appropriate. For example: `SUM(Price*7)` and `SUM(Price)*7` are both valid expressions.
- All of the functions can be evaluated on aggregated values. However, the arguments to any given function must either all be aggregated or all disaggregated. For example: `MAX(SUM(Sales),Profit)` is not a valid expression because Sales is aggregated and Profit is not. However, `MAX(SUM(Sales),SUM(Profit))` is a valid expression.
- The result of an aggregate calculation is always a measure. This includes expressions like ATTR(Dimension) or MIN(Dimension).
- Like predefined aggregations, aggregate calculations are computed correctly for grand totals. Refer to Grand Totals for more information.

# Alibaba AnalyticDB for MySQL

This topic describes how to connect Tableau to an Alibaba AnalyticDB for MySQL database and set up the data source.

## Before you begin

Before you begin, gather this connection information:

- Name or IP address of the server that hosts the database you want to connect to
- Database name
- User name and password
- (Optional) Initial SQL statement to run every time Tableau connects

### Driver required

This connector requires a driver to talk to the database. If the driver is not installed on your computer, Tableau displays a message in the connection dialog box with a link to the [Driver Download](https://www.tableau.com/support/drivers) page where you can find driver links and installation instructions.

## Make the connection and set up the data source

1. Start Tableau and under Connect, select Alibaba AnalyticDB for MySQL. For a complete list of data connections, select More under To a Server. Then do the following:
    
    1. Enter the Server name or IP address.
    2. Enter the Database name.
    3. Enter the Username and Password.
    4. (Optional) Select Initial SQL to specify a SQL command to run at the beginning of every connection, such as when you open the workbook, refresh an extract, sign in to Tableau Server, or publish to Tableau Server. For more information, see [Run Initial SQL](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/connect_basic_initialsql.htm).
    5. Select Sign In.
        
        If Tableau can't make the connection, verify that your credentials are correct. If you still can't connect, your computer is having trouble locating the server. Contact your network administrator or database administrator for more assistance.
2. On the data source page, do the following:
    
    1. (Optional) Select the default data source name at the top of the page, and then enter a unique data source name for use in Tableau. For example, use a data source naming convention that helps other users of the data source figure out which data source to connect to.
    2. Under Table, select a table or use the text box to search for a table by name.
    3. Drag the table to the canvas, and then select the sheet tab to start your analysis.
        
        Use custom SQL to connect to a specific query rather than the entire data source. For more information, see [Connect to a Custom SQL Query](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/customsql.htm).

## Sign in on a Mac

If you use Tableau Desktop on a Mac, when you enter the server name to connect, use a fully qualified domain name, such as mydb.test.ourdomain.lan, instead of a relative domain name, such as mydb or mydb.test.

Alternatively, you can add the domain to the list of Search Domains for the Mac computer so that when you connect, you need to provide only the server name. To update the list of Search Domains, go to System Preferences > Network > Advanced, and then open the DNS tab.

## See also

- [Set Up Data Sources](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/datasource_prepare.htm) – Add more data to this data source or prepare your data before you analyze it.
- [Build Charts and Analyze Data](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/design_and_analyze.htm) – Begin your data analysis.

## A

### ABS

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>ABS(number)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Number (positive)</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the absolute value of the given <code>&lt;number&gt;</code>.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>ABS(-7) = 7<br>ABS([Budget Variance])</pre>
                                <p>The second example returns the absolute value for all the numbers contained in the Budget Variance field.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>

### AND

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>&lt;expr1&gt; AND &lt;expr2&gt;</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Performs a logical conjunction on two expressions. (If both sides are true, the logical test returns true.)</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Boolean </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Spring" AND "[Season] = "Fall" <br>THEN "It's the apocalypse and footwear doesn't matter" <br>END</pre>
                                <p><i>"If both (Season = Spring) and (Season = Fall) are true simultaneously, then return It's the apocalypse and footwear doesn't matter."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Often used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. See also <a href="#NOT" class="xref">NOT</a> and <a href="#OR" class="xref">OR</a>. </p>
                                <p>If both expressions are <code>TRUE</code> (that is, not <code>FALSE</code> or <code>NULL</code>), then the result is <code>TRUE</code>. If either expression is <code>NULL</code>, then the result is <code>NULL</code>. In all other cases, the result is <code>FALSE</code>.</p>
                                <p>If you create a calculation in which the result of an <code>AND</code> comparison is displayed on a worksheet, Tableau displays <code>TRUE</code> and <code>FALSE</code>. If you would like to change this, use the Format area in the format dialog.</p>
                                <p class="note"><b>Note</b>: The <code>AND</code> operator employs <i>short circuit evaluation</i>. This means that if the first expression is evaluated to be <code>FALSE</code>, then the second expression is not evaluated at all. This can be helpful if the second expression results in an error when the first expression is <code>FALSE</code>, because the second expression in this case is never evaluated.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

## C

### CASE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code><b>CASE</b> &lt;expression&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; 
							<br>...
						<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Depends on data type of the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>&nbsp;values. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Evaluates the <code>expression</code> and compares it to the specified options (<code>&lt;value1&gt;</code>, <code>&lt;value2&gt;</code>, etc.). When a <code>value</code> that matches expression is encountered, CASE returns the corresponding <code>return</code>. If no match is found, the (optional) default is returned. If there is no default and no values match, then Null is returned.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre><code><b>CASE</b> [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</code></pre>
                                <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. </p>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a>. </p>
                                <blockquote><p>[!TIP]</p><p>Many times you can use a group to get the same results as a complicated CASE function, or use CASE to replace native grouping functionality, such as in the previous example. You may want to test which is more performant for your scenario.</p></blockquote>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### CORR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>CORR(expression1, expression2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Number from -1 to 1</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the Pearson correlation coefficient of two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>example</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>The Pearson correlation measures the linear relationship between two variables. Results range from -1 to +1 inclusive, where 1 denotes an exact positive linear relationship, 0 denotes no linear relationship between the variance, and −1 is an exact negative relationship.</p>
                                <p>The square of a CORR result is equivalent to the R-Squared value for a linear trend line model. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/trendlines_add.htm#Terms" target="_blank">Trend Line Model Terms</a>.</p>
                                <p><b>Use with table scoped LOD&nbsp;expressions:</b>
                                </p>
                                <p>You can use CORR to visualize correlation in a disaggregated scatter using a <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_calculatedfields_lod.htm#Table" target="_blank">table-scoped level of detail expression</a>. For example:</p><pre>{CORR(Sales, Profit)}</pre>
                                <p>With a level of detail expression, the correlation is run over all rows. If you used a formula like <code>CORR(Sales, Profit)</code> (without the surrounding brackets to make it a level of detail expression), the view would show the correlation of each individual point in the scatter plot with each other point, which is undefined.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>CORR</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica.</p>
                                <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_CORR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### COVAR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>COVAR(expression1, expression2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the <i>sample</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Sample covariance</i> uses the number of non-null data points n - 1 to normalize the covariance calculation, rather than n, which is used by the population covariance (available with the <code>COVARP</code> function). Sample covariance is the appropriate choice when the data is a random sample that is being used to estimate the covariance for a larger population.</p>
                                <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVAR([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVAR</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed.</p>
                                <p>The value of <code>COVAR(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VAR(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEV(X)^2</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>COVAR</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica.</p>
                                <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### COVARP

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>COVARP(expression 1, expression2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the <i>population</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Population covariance</i> is sample covariance multiplied by (n-1)/n, where n is the total number of non-null data points. Population covariance is the appropriate choice when there is data available for all items of interest as opposed to when there is only a random subset of items, in which case sample covariance (with the <code>COVAR</code> function) is appropriate.</p>
                                <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVARP([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVARP</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed. Note: The value of <code>COVARP(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VARP(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEVP(X)^2</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>COVARP</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica</p>
                                <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

## D

### DATE

Type conversion function that changes string and number expressions into dates, as long as they are in a recognizable format.

<table class="table--plain">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATE(expression)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Date</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns a date given a number, string, or date <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code>.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>DATE([Employee Start Date])</pre><pre>DATE("September 22, 2018") </pre><pre>DATE("9/22/2018")</pre><pre>DATE(#2018-09-22 14:52#)</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Unlike <code><a href="#DATEPARSE" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a></code>, there is no need to provide a pattern as <code>DATE</code> automatically recognizes many standard date formats. If <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input, however, try using <code>DATEPARSE</code> and specifying the format.</p>
                                <p><code><a href="#MAKEDATE" class="xref">MAKEDATE</a></code> is another similar function, but <code>MAKEDATE</code> requires the input of numeric values for year, month, and day.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### DATEADD

Adds a specified number of date parts (months, days, etc) to the starting date.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATEADD(date_part, interval, date)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Date</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the specified date with the specified number <code>&lt;interval&gt;</code> added to the specified &gt;<code>&lt;date_part</code> of that date. For example, adding three months or 12 days to a starting date.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Push out all due dates by one week</p><pre>DATEADD('week', 1, [due date])</pre>
                                <p>Add 280 days to the date February 20, 2021</p><pre>DATEADD('day', 280, #2/20/21#) = #November 27, 2021#</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### DATEDIFF

Returns the number of date parts (weeks, years, etc) between two dates.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATEDIFF(date_part, date1, date2, [start_of_week])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Integer</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the difference between <code>date1</code> and <code>date2</code> expressed in units of <code>date_part</code>. For example, subtracting the dates someone entered and left a band to see how long they were in the band.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Number of days between March 25, 1986 and February 20, 2021</p><pre>DATEDIFF('day', #3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = 12,751</pre>
                                <p>How many months someone was in a band</p><pre>DATEDIFF('month', [date joined band], [date left band])</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### DATENAME

Returns the name of the specified date part as a discrete string.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATENAME(date_part, date, [start_of_week])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>String</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns <code>&lt;date_part&gt;</code> of date as a string.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>DATENAME('year', #3/25/1986#) = "1986"</pre><pre>DATENAME('month', #1986-03-25#) = "March"</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</p>
                                <p>A very similar calculation is <a href="#DATEPART" class="xref">DATEPART</a>, which returns the value of the specified date part as a continuous integer. <code>DATEPART</code> can be faster because it is a numerical operation.</p>
                                <p>By changing the attributes of the calculation’s result (dimension or measure, continuous or discrete) and the date formatting, the results of <code>DATEPART</code> and <code>DATENAME</code> can be formatted to be identical.</p>
                                <p>An inverse function is <code><a href="#DATEPARSE" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a></code>, which takes a string value and formats it as a date.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### DATEPARSE

Returns specifically formatted strings as dates.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATEPARSE(date_format, date_string)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Date</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>The <code>&lt;date_format&gt;</code> argument describes how the <code>&lt;date_string&gt;</code> field is arranged. Because of the variety of ways the string field can be ordered, the <code>&lt;date_format&gt;</code> must match exactly. For a full explanation, see <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/data_dateparse.htm" target="_blank">Convert a Field to a Date Field</a>.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>DATEPARSE('yyyy-MM-dd', "1986-03-25") = #March 25, 1986#</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code><a href="#DATE" class="xref">DATE</a></code> is a similar function that automatically recognizes many standard date formats.  <code>DATEPARSE</code> may be a better option if <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input pattern. </p>
                                <p><code><a href="#MAKEDATE" class="xref">MAKEDATE</a></code> is another similar function, but <code>MAKEDATE</code> requires the input of numeric values for year, month, and day. </p>
                                <p>Inverse functions, which take dates apart and return the value of their parts, are <code><a href="#DATEPART" class="xref">DATEPART</a></code> (integer output) and <code><a href="#DATENAME" class="xref">DATENAME</a></code> (string output). </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>DATEPARSE</code> is available through the following connectors: non-legacy Excel and text file connections, Amazon EMR Hadoop Hive, Cloudera Hadoop, Google Sheets, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, MapR Hadoop Hive, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Tableau extracts. Some formats may not be available for all connections.</p>
                                <p><code>DATEPARSE</code> is not supported on Hive variants. Only Denodo, Drill, and Snowflake are supported.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### DATETRUNC

This function can be thought of as date rounding. It takes a specific date and returns a version of that date at the desired specificity. Because every date must have a value for day, month, quarter, and year, `DATETRUNC` sets the values as the lowest value for each date part up to the date part specified. Refer to the example for more information.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>DATETRUNC(date_part, date, [start_of_week])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Date</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Truncates the <code>&lt;date&gt;</code> to the accuracy specified by the <code>&lt;date_part&gt;</code>. This function returns a new date. For example, when you truncate a date that is in the middle of the month at the month level, this function returns the first day of the month. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>DATETRUNC('day', #9/22/2018#) = #9/22/2018#</pre><pre>DATETRUNC('iso-week', #9/22/2018#) = #9/17/2018#</pre>
                                <p>(the monday of the week containing 9/22/2018)</p><pre>DATETRUNC(quarter, #9/22/2018#) = #7/1/2018# </pre>
                                <p>(the first day of the quarter containing 9/22/2018)</p>
                                <p class="note">Note: For week and iso-week, the <code>start_of_week</code> comes into play. ISO-weeks always start on Monday. For the locale of this example, an unspecified <code>start_of_week</code> means the week starts on Sunday.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</p>
                                <p>You shouldn't use <code>DATETRUNC</code> to, for example, stop showing the time for a datetime field in a viz.  If you want to truncate the <i>display</i> of a date rather than round its accuracy, <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/dates_custom_date_formats.htm" target="_blank">adjust the formatting</a>. </p>
                                <p>For example, <code>DATETRUNC('day', #5/17/2022 3:12:48 PM#)</code>,  if formatted in the viz to display seconds, would display as <code>5/17/2022 12:00:00 AM</code>. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

## E

### ELSE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>CASE &lt;expression&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; 
							<br>...
						<br>[<b>ELSE</b> &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>An optional piece of an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;or <code>CASE</code> expression used to specify a default value to return if none of the tested expressions are true. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br><b>ELSE</b>&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br>END</pre><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br><b>ELSE</b> 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>,  and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                <p><code>ELSE</code> is optional with <code>CASE</code> and <code>IF</code>. In a calculation where <code>ELSE</code> is not specified, if none of the <code>&lt;test&gt;</code>are true, the overall calculation will return null. </p>
                                <p><code>ELSE</code> does not require a condition (such as <code>[Season] = "Winter"</code>) and can be thought of as a form of null handling. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### ELSEIF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>[<b>ELSEIF</b> &lt;test2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt;]</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>An optional piece of an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;expression used to specify additional conditions beyond the initial IF.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Summer" THEN 'Sandals' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Winter" THEN 'Boots' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Spring" THEN 'Sneakers' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Autumn" THEN 'Sneakers'<br>ELSE 'Bare feet' <br>END</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>,  <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                <p><code>ELSEIF</code> can be thought of as additional <code>IF</code> clauses. <code>ELSEIF</code> is optional and can be repeated multiple times. </p>
                                <p>Unlike <code>ELSE</code>, <code>ELSEIF</code> requires a condition (such as <code>[Season] = "Winter"</code>).</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### END

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Used to close an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;or <code>CASE</code> expression. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br><b>END</b></pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                </p><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br><b>END</b></pre>
                                <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, and <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

Hexagonal bins are an efficient and elegant option for visualizing data in an x/y plane such as a map. Because the bins are hexagonal, each bin closely approximates a circle and minimizes variation in the distance from the data point to the center of the bin. This makes the clustering both more accurate and informative.</td>

## I

### IF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code><b>IF</b> &lt;test1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; <br>[ELSEIF &lt;test2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt;...]<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;] <br>END</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Depends on data type of the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>&nbsp;values. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Tests a series of expressions  and returns the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code> value for the first true <code>&lt;test&gt;</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br><b>END</b></pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. </p>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### IFNULL

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>IFNULL(expr1, expr2)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Depends on the data type of the <code>&lt;expr&gt;</code> values. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Returns <code>&lt;expr1&gt;</code> if it's non-null, otherwise returns <code>&lt;expr2&gt;</code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IFNULL([Assigned Room], "TBD")</pre>
                                <p><i>"If the Assigned Room field isn't null, return its value. If the Assigned room field is null, return TBD instead."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Compare with <a href="#ISNULL" class="xref">ISNULL</a>. <code>IFNULL</code> always returns a value. <code>ISNULL</code>&nbsp;returns a boolean (true or false). </p>
                                <p>See also <a href="#ZN" class="xref">ZN</a>. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### IIF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code><b>IIF</b>(&lt;test&gt;, &lt;then&gt;, &lt;else&gt;, [&lt;unknown&gt;])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Depends on the data type of the values in the expression. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Checks whether a condition is met (<code>&lt;test&gt;</code>), and returns <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>if the test is true, <code>&lt;else&gt;</code>&nbsp;if the test is false, and an optional  value for <code>&lt;unknown&gt;</code> if the test is null. If the optional unknown isn't specified, <code>IIF</code> returns null. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IIF([Season] = 'Summer', 'Sandals', 'Other footwear')</pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, return Other footwear"</i>
                                </p><pre>IIF([Season] = 'Summer', 'Sandals', <br>   IIF('Season' = 'Winter', 'Boots',  'Other footwear')<br>)</pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                </p><pre>IIF('Season' = 'Summer', 'Sandals', <br>   IIF('Season' = 'Winter', 'Boots',  <br>      IIF('Season' = 'Spring', 'Sneakers', 'Other footwear')<br>   )<br>)</pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If none of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and<a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>. </p>
                                <p><code>IIF</code> doesn't have an equivalent to <code>ELSEIF</code> (like <code>IF</code>)&nbsp;or repeated <code>WHEN</code> clauses (like <code>CASE</code>). Instead, multiple tests can be evaluated sequentially by nesting <code>IIF</code> statements as the <code>&lt;unknown&gt;</code>&nbsp;element. The first (outermost) true  is returned. </p>
                                <p>That is to say, in the calculation below,  the result will be Red, not Orange, because the expression stops being evaluated as soon as A=A is evaluated as true: </p>
                                <p> <code>IIF('A' = 'A', 'Red', IIF('B' = 'B', 'Orange',  IIF('C' = 'D', 'Yellow', 'Green')))</code></p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">

                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>

### MAKEDATE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>

                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>

                        </tr>
                        <tr>

                            </td>
                        </tr>

                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p class="note"><b>Note</b>: Incorrectly entered values will be adjusted into a date, such as <code>MAKEDATE(2020,4,31) = May 1, 2020</code> rather than returning an error that there is no 31st day of April.</p>
                                <p>Available for Tableau Data Extracts. Check for availability in other data sources.</p>
                                <p><code>MAKEDATE</code> requires numerical inputs for the parts of a date. If your data is a string that should be a date, try the <code><a href="#DATE" class="xref">DATE</a></code> function. <code>DATE</code> automatically recognizes many standard date formats. If <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input try using <code><a href="#DATEPARSE" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a></code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### MAKEPOINT

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>MAKEPOINT(latitude, longitude, [SRID])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Geometry (point)</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Converts data from <code>&lt;latitude&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;longitude&gt;</code> columns into spatial objects.</p>
                                <p>If the optional <code>&lt;SRID&gt;</code> argument is added, the inputs can be other projected geographic coordinates. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>MAKEPOINT(48.5, -123.1)</pre><pre>MAKEPOINT([AirportLatitude], [AirportLongitude])</pre><pre>MAKEPOINT([Xcoord],[Ycoord], 3493)</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>MAKEPOINT</code> can't use the automatically generated latitude and longitude fields. The data source must contain the  coordinates natively. </p>
                                <p>SRID is a spatial reference identifier that uses <a href="https://epsg.io/" target="_blank">ESPG reference system codes</a> to specify coordinate systems. If SRID is not specified, WGS84 is assumed and parameters are treated as latitude/longitude in degrees.</p>
                                <p>You can use <code>MAKEPOINT</code> to spatially-enable a data source so that it can be joined with a spatial file using a spatial join. For more information, see <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/maps_spatial_join.htm" target="_blank">Join Spatial Files in Tableau</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>MAKETIME(14, 52, 40) = #1/1/1899 14:52:40#</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Because Tableau does not support a time data type, only datetime, the output is a datetime. The date portion of the field will be 1/1/1899.</p>
                                <p>Similar function to <code><a href="#MAKEDATETIME" class="xref">MAKEDATETIME</a></code>, which is only available for MYSQL-compatible connections.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><b>For strings</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                <p><b>For dates</b>
                                </p>
                                <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                </p>
                                <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### MEDIAN

                        </tr>
                        <tr>

                            <td>
                                <p><code>MEDIAN</code> is <b>not</b> available for the following data sources: Access, Amazon Redshift, Cloudera Hadoop, HP Vertica, IBM DB2, IBM PDA (Netezza), Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, SAP HANA, Teradata.</p>
                                <p>For other data source types, you can extract your data into an extract file to use this function. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/extracting_data.htm" target="_blank">Extract Your Data</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### Model Extensions

For more information, see [Table Calculation Functions](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm).

- MODEL\_EXTENSION\_INT

### MODEL\_PERCENTILE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>MODEL_PERCENTILE(
							<br>model_specification (optional),
							<br>target_expression,
						<br>predictor_expression(s))</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns the probability (between 0 and 1) of the expected value being less than or equal to the observed mark, defined by the target expression and other predictors. This is the Posterior Predictive Distribution Function, also known as the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF).</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>MODEL_PERCENTILE( SUM([Sales]),COUNT([Orders]))</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### MODEL\_QUANTILE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>MODEL_QUANTILE(
							<br>model_specification (optional), 
							<br>quantile, 
							<br>target_expression,
						<br>predictor_expression(s))</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns a target numeric value within the probable range defined by the target expression and other predictors, at a specified quantile. This is the Posterior Predictive Quantile.
					</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>MODEL_QUANTILE(0.5, SUM([Sales]), COUNT([Orders]))</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>
