## O

### OR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>&lt;expr1&gt; OR &lt;expr2&gt;</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Performs a logical disjunction on two expressions.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Spring"&nbsp;<b>OR</b>&nbsp;[Season] = "Fall" <br>THEN&nbsp;"Sneakers" <br>END</pre>
                                <p><i>"If either (Season = Spring)&nbsp;or (Season = Fall)&nbsp;is true, then return Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Often used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. See also <a href="#top" class="xref">The Tableau functions in this reference are organized alphabetically. Click a letter to jump to that location in the list. You can also use Ctrl+F (Command-F on a Mac) to open a search box to look for a specific function.</a> and <a href="#NOT" class="xref">NOT</a>.</p>
                                <p>If either expression
							is <code>TRUE</code>, then the result is <code>TRUE</code>.
							If both expressions are <code>FALSE</code>, then the result
							is <code>FALSE</code>. If both expressions are <code>NULL</code>,
						then the result is <code>NULL</code>. </p>
                                <p>If you create
							a calculation which displays the result of an <code>OR</code> comparison
							on a worksheet, Tableau displays <code>TRUE</code>and <code>FALSE</code>. If
							you would like to change this, use the Format area in the format
						dialog. </p>
                                <p class="note"><b>Note</b>:&nbsp;The <code>OR</code> operator employs <em>short circuit
							evaluation.</em> This means that if the first expression is evaluated
							to be <code>TRUE</code>, then the second expression is not evaluated
							at all. This can be helpful if the second expression results in
							an error when the first expression is <code>TRUE</code>, because
						the second expression in this case is never evaluated.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### RANK Table Calculation functions

### ROUND

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>ROUND(number, [decimals])</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Number</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Rounds the <code>&lt;number&gt;</code> to a specified number of digits. </p>
                                <p>The optional <code>decimals</code> argument specifies how many decimal points of precision to include in the final result. If <code>decimals</code> is omitted, number is rounded to the nearest integer.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>ROUND(1/3, 2) = 0.33</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Some databases, such as SQL Server, allow specification of a negative length, where -1 rounds number to the tens place, -2 rounds to the hundreds place, and so on. This is not true of all databases. For example, it is not true of Excel or Access.</p>
                                <blockquote><p>[!TIP]</p><p>Because ROUND may run into issues due to the underlying floating point representation of numbers—such as 9.405 rounding to 9.40—it may be preferable to <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/formatting_specific_numbers.htm">format the number</a> to the desired number of decimal points rather than rounding. Formatting 9.405 to two decimal places will yield the expected 9.41.</p></blockquote>
                                <p>See also <code><a href="#CEILING" class="xref">CEILING</a></code> and <code><a href="#FLOOR" class="xref">FLOOR</a></code>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### SPLIT

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>SPLIT(string, delimiter, token number)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>String</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns a substring from a <code>&lt;string&gt;</code>, using a <code>&lt;delimiter&gt;</code> character to divide the string into a sequence of <code>&lt;tokens&gt;</code>.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>SPLIT ("a-b-c-d", "-", 2) = "b"</pre><pre>SPLIT ("a|b|c|d", "|", -2) = "c"</pre>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>The string is interpreted as an alternating sequence of delimiters and tokens. So for the string <code>abc-defgh-i-jkl</code>, where the delimiter character is '<code>-</code>', the tokens are (1) <code>abc</code>, (2) <code>defgh</code>, (3) <code>i</code>, and (4) <code>jlk</code>.</p>
                                <p><code>SPLIT</code> returns the token corresponding to the token number. When the token number is positive, tokens are counted starting from the left end of the string; when the token number is negative, tokens are counted starting from the right.</p>
                                <p>See also supported REGEX in the <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_additional.htm" target="_blank">additional functions documentation</a>. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Database limitations</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>The split and custom split commands are available for the following data sources types: Tableau data extracts, Microsoft Excel, Text File, PDF File, Salesforce, OData, Microsoft Azure Market Place, Google Analytics, Vertica, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Teradata, Amazon Redshift, Aster Data, Google Big Query, Cloudera Hadoop Hive, Hortonworks Hive, and Microsoft SQL Server.</p>
                                <p>Some data sources impose limits on splitting strings. See SPLIT&nbsp;function limitations later in this topic. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### THEN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>IF &lt;test1&gt; <b>THEN</b> &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br>[ELSEIF &lt;test2&gt; <b>THEN</b> &lt;then2&gt;...]
							<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;] 
						<br>END</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>A required part of an <code>IF</code>, <code>ELSEIF</code>, or <code>CASE</code> expression, used to define what result to return if a specific value or test is true. </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;<b>THEN</b>&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;<b>THEN</b>&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br>END</pre>
                                <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i> </p><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' <b>THEN</b> 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' <b>THEN</b> 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                                <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### USERNAME

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">

                            <td>String</td>

                        </tr>
                        <tr>

                            <td><pre xml:space="preserve">USERNAME( )</pre>
                                <p>This returns the username of the signed in user, such as "hmyrer".</p><pre xml:space="preserve">[Manager] = USERNAME( )</pre>
                                <p>If manager "hmyrer" is signed in, this example returns TRUE only if the Manager field in the view contains "hmyrer". </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>This function checks:</p>
                                <ul>
                                    <li><span class="mc-variable Variables.TabsProductOnline variable">Tableau Cloud</span> and <span class="mc-variable Variables.TabsProductServer variable">Tableau Server</span>:&nbsp;the username of the signed-in user</li>
                                    <li><span class="mc-variable Variables.TabsProductDesktop variable">Tableau Desktop</span>: the local or network username for the user</li>
                                </ul>
                                <p><b>User filters</b>
                                </p>
                                <p>When used as a filter, a calculated field such as <code>[Username field] = USERNAME( )</code> can be used to create a user filter that only shows data that is relevant to the person signed in to the server.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>

### WHEN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>CASE &lt;expression&gt;<br><b>WHEN</b> &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt;<br><b>WHEN</b> &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt;<br>...<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>A required part of a <code>CASE</code> expression. Finds the first <code>&lt;value&gt;</code> that matches <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code> and returns the corresponding <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre>CASE [Season] <br><b>WHEN</b> 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br><b>WHEN</b> 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                                <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a>. </p>
                                <p><code>CASE</code> also supports <code>WHEN IN</code> construction, such as:</p><pre xml:space="preserve">CASE &lt;expression&gt; <br><b>WHEN IN</b> &lt;set1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; <br><b>WHEN IN</b> &lt;combinedfield&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; <br>... <br>ELSE &lt;default&gt; <br>END</pre>
                                <p>The values that <code>WHEN IN</code> compare to must be a set, list of literal values, or combined field. See also <a href="#IN" class="xref">IN</a>.</p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

## Z

### ZN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                    <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                    <col>
                    </colgroup><tbody>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Syntax</td>
                            <td><code>ZN(expression)</code>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Output</td>
                            <td>Depends on the data type of the <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code>, or 0.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Definition</td>
                            <td>Returns <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code> if it isn't null, otherwise returns zero.</td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Example</td>
                            <td><pre xml:space="preserve">ZN([Test Grade])</pre>
                                <p><i>"If the test grade isn't null, return its value. If the test grade is null, return 0."</i>
                                </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                        <tr>
                            <td>Notes</td>
                            <td>
                                <p><code>ZN</code> is a specialized case of <a href="#IFNULL" class="xref">IFNULL</a> where alternative if the expression is null is always 0 rather than being specified in the calculation. </p>
                                <p><code>ZN</code> is especially useful when performing additional calculations and a null would render the entire calculation null. However, use caution interpreting these results as null is not always synonymous with 0 and could represent missing data. </p>
                                <p>See also <a href="#ISNULL" class="xref">ISNULL</a>. </p>
                            </td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>

### HEXBINX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>HEXBINX(number, number)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Number</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Maps an x, y coordinate to the x-coordinate of the nearest hexagonal bin. The bins have side length 1, so the inputs may need to be scaled appropriately.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">HEXBINX([Longitude]*2.5, [Latitude]*2.5)</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td><code>HEXBINX </code>and <code><a href="#HEXBINY" class="xref">HEXBINY</a></code> are binning and plotting functions for hexagonal bins. Hexagonal bins are an efficient and elegant option for visualizing data in an x/y plane such as a map. Because the bins are hexagonal, each bin closely approximates a circle and minimizes variation in the distance from the data point to the center of the bin. This makes the clustering both more accurate and informative.</td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MIN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MIN(expression)</code> or <code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the minimum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN </code>can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MIN(4,7) = 4<br>MIN(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #3/25/1986#<br>MIN([Name]) = "Abebi"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN</code> is usually the value that comes first in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MIN</code> string value is lowest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MIN</code> is the earliest date. If <code>MIN</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MIN</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MAX" class="xref">MAX</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ROUND

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>ROUND(number, [decimals])</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Number</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Rounds <code>&lt;number&gt;</code> to a specified number of digits. </p>
                                        <p>The optional <code>decimals</code> argument specifies how many decimal points of precision to include in the final result. If <code>decimals</code> is omitted, number is rounded to the nearest integer.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">ROUND(1/3, 2) = 0.33</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Some databases, such as SQL Server, allow specification of a negative length, where -1 rounds number to 10's, -2 rounds to 100's, and so on. This is not true of all databases. For example, it is not true of Excel or Access.

</p>
                                        <blockquote><p>[!TIP]</p><p>Because <code>ROUND</code> may run into issues due to the underlying floating point representation of numbers—such as 9.405 rounding to 9.40—it may be preferable to <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/formatting_specific_numbers.htm">format the number</a> to the desired number of decimal points rather than rounding. Formatting 9.405 to two decimal places will yield the expected 9.41.</p></blockquote>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#CEILING" class="xref">CEILING</a></code> and <code><a href="#FLOOR" class="xref">FLOOR</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ZN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>ZN(expression)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Any, or o</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code> if it is not null, otherwise returns zero. </p>
                                        <p>Use this function to replace null values with zeros.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">ZN(Grade) = 0</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>This is a very useful function when using fields that may contain nulls in a calculation. Wrapping the field with <code>ZN</code> can prevent errors caused by calculating with nulls. </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

String functions

### ASCII

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

                                </tr>
                                <tr>

                                    </td>

                                </tr>
                            </tbody>

### MIN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>

                                    <td>Syntax</td>

                                </tr>

                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the minimum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN </code>can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>

                                        <p><b>For dates</b>

### PROPER

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">

### SPLIT

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>SPLIT(string, delimiter, token number)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>String</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns a substring from a string, using a delimiter character to divide the string into a sequence of tokens.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>SPLIT ("a-b-c-d", "-", 2) = "b"</pre><pre>SPLIT ("a|b|c|d", "|", -2) = "c"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>The string is interpreted as an alternating sequence of delimiters and tokens. So for the string <code>abc-defgh-i-jkl</code>, where the delimiter character is '<code>-</code>', the tokens are (1) <code>abc</code>, (2) <code>defgh</code>, (3) <code>i</code>, and (4) <code>jlk</code>.</p>
                                        <p><code>SPLIT</code> returns the token corresponding to the token number. When the token number is positive, tokens are counted starting from the left end of the string; when the token number is negative, tokens are counted starting from the right.</p>
                                        <p>See also supported REGEX in the <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_additional.htm" target="_blank">additional functions documentation</a>. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Database limitations</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>The split and custom split commands are available for the following data sources types: Tableau data extracts, Microsoft Excel, Text File, PDF File, Salesforce, OData, Microsoft Azure Market Place, Google Analytics, Vertica, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Teradata, Amazon Redshift, Aster Data, Google Big Query, Cloudera Hadoop Hive, Hortonworks Hive, and Microsoft SQL Server.</p>
                                        <p>Some data sources impose limits on splitting strings. See SPLIT&nbsp;function limitations later in this topic. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### STARTSWITH

Date functions

**Note**: Date functions do not take account of the configured fiscal year start. See [Fiscal Dates](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/dates_fiscal.htm).

### DATE

Type conversion function that changes string and number expressions into dates, as long as they are in a recognizable format.

<table class="table--plain">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATE(expression)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Date</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns a date given a number, string, or date <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code>.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>DATE([Employee Start Date])</pre><pre>DATE("September 22, 2018") </pre><pre xml:space="preserve">DATE("9/22/2018")</pre><pre>DATE(#2018-09-22 14:52#)</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Unlike <code><a href="#DATEPARS" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a></code>, there is no need to provide a pattern as <code>DATE</code> automatically recognizes many standard date formats. If <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input, however, try using <code>DATEPARSE</code> and specifying the format. </p>
                                        <p><code><a href="#MAKEDATE" class="xref">MAKEDATE</a></code> is another similar function, but <code>MAKEDATE</code> requires the input of numeric values for year, month, and day.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### DATEADD

Adds a specified number of date parts (months, days, etc) to the starting date.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATEADD(date_part, interval, date)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Date</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns the <code>&lt;date&gt;</code> with the specified number <code>&lt;interval&gt;</code> added to the specified <code>&lt;<a href="#arg" class="xref">date_part</a>&gt;</code> of that date. For example, adding three months or 12 days to a starting date.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Push out all due dates by one week</p><pre>DATEADD('week', 1, [due date])</pre>
                                        <p>Add 280 days to the date February 20, 2021</p><pre xml:space="preserve">DATEADD('day', 280, #2/20/21#) = #November 27, 2021#</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### DATEDIFF

Returns the number of date parts (weeks, years, etc) between two dates.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATEDIFF(date_part, date1, date2, [start_of_week])</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Integer</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns the difference between <code>&lt;date1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;date2&gt;</code> expressed in units of <code>&lt;<a href="#arg" class="xref">date_part</a>&gt;</code>. For example, subtracting the dates someone entered and left a band to see how long they were in the band.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Number of days between March 25, 1986 and February 20, 2021
</p><pre>DATEDIFF('day', #3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = 12,751</pre>
                                        <p>How many months someone was in a band
</p><pre>DATEDIFF('month', [date joined band], [date left band])</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### DATENAME

Returns the name of the specified date part as a discrete string.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATENAME(date_part, date, [start_of_week])</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>String</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns <code>&lt;<a href="#arg" class="xref">date_part</a>&gt;</code> of <code>&lt;date&gt;</code> as a string.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>DATENAME('year', #3/25/1986#) = "1986"</pre><pre>DATENAME('month', #1986-03-25#) = "March"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</p>
                                        <p>A very similar calculation is <a href="#DATEPART" class="xref">DATEPART</a>, which returns the value of the specified date part as a continuous integer. <code>DATEPART</code> can be faster because it is a numerical operation. </p>
                                        <p>By changing the attributes of the calculation’s result (dimension or measure, continuous or discrete) and the date formatting, the results of <code>DATEPART</code> and <code>DATENAME</code> can be formatted to be identical. </p>
                                        <p>An inverse function is <a href="#DATEPARS" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a>, which takes a string value and formats it as a date.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### DATEPARSE

Returns specifically formatted strings as dates.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATEPARSE(date_format, date_string)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Date</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>The <code>&lt;date_format&gt;</code> argument describes how the <code>&lt;date_string&gt;</code> field is arranged. Because of the variety of ways the string field can be ordered, the <code>&lt;date_format&gt;</code> must match exactly. For a full explanation and formatting details, see <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/data_dateparse.htm" target="_blank">Convert a Field to a Date Field</a>.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">DATEPARSE('yyyy-MM-dd', "1986-03-25") = #March 25, 1986#</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><code><a href="#top" class="xref">DATE</a></code> is a similar function that automatically recognizes many standard date formats.  <code>DATEPARSE</code> may be a better option if <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input pattern. </p>
                                        <p><code><a href="#MAKEDATE" class="xref">MAKEDATE</a></code> is another similar function, but <code>MAKEDATE</code> requires the input of numeric values for year, month, and day. </p>
                                        <p>Inverse functions, which take dates apart and return the value of their parts, are <code><a href="#DATEPART" class="xref">DATEPART</a></code> (integer output) and <code><a href="#DATENAME" class="xref">DATENAME</a></code> (string output). </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Database limitations</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><code>DATEPARSE</code> is available through the following connectors: non-legacy Excel and text file connections, Amazon EMR Hadoop Hive, Cloudera Hadoop, Google Sheets, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, MapR Hadoop Hive, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, and Tableau extracts. Some formats may not be available for all connections.</p>
                                        <p><code>DATEPARSE</code> is not supported on Hive variants. Only Denodo, Drill, and Snowflake are supported.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

By changing the attributes of the field (dimension or measure, continuous or discrete) and the date formatting, the results of <code>DATEPART</code> and <code>DATENAME</code> can be formatted to be identical. </p>

### DATETRUNC

This function can be thought of as date rounding. It takes a specific date and returns a version of that date at the desired specificity. Because every date must have a value for day, month, quarter, and year, `DATETRUNC` sets the values as the lowest value for each date part up to the date part specified. Refer to the example for more information.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>DATETRUNC(date_part, date, [start_of_week])</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Date</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Truncates the <code>&lt;date&gt;</code> to the accuracy specified by the <code>&lt;<a href="#arg" class="xref">date_part</a>&gt;</code>. This function returns a new date. For example, when you truncate a date that is in the middle of the month at the month level, this function returns the first day of the month. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">DATETRUNC('day', #9/22/2018#) = #9/22/2018#</pre><pre xml:space="preserve">DATETRUNC('iso-week', #9/22/2018#) = #9/17/2018#</pre>
                                        <p>(the monday of the week containing 9/22/2018)</p><pre xml:space="preserve">DATETRUNC(quarter, #9/22/2018#) = #7/1/2018# </pre>
                                        <p>(the first day of the quarter containing 9/22/2018)</p>
                                        <p class="note">Note: For week and iso-week, the <code>start_of_week</code> comes into play. ISO-weeks always start on Monday. For the locale of this example, an unspecified <code>start_of_week</code> means the week starts on Sunday.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Supports ISO 8601 dates.</p>
                                        <p>You shouldn't use <code>DATETRUNC</code> to, for example, stop showing the time for a datetime field in a viz.  If you want to truncate the way a date displays rather than round its accuracy, <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/dates_custom_date_formats.htm" target="_blank">adjust the formatting</a>. </p>
                                        <p>For example, <code>DATETRUNC('day', #5/17/2022 3:12:48 PM#)</code>,  if formatted in the viz to display seconds, would display as <code>5/17/2022 12:00:00 AM</code>. The value is truncated to day, but the display goes to seconds. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MAKEDATE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAKEDATE(year, month, day)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Date</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns a date value constructed from the specified <code>&lt;year&gt;</code>, <code>&lt;month&gt;</code>, and <code>&lt;day&gt;</code>.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAKEDATE(1986,3,25) = #1986-03-25#</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p class="note"><b>Note</b>: Incorrectly entered values will be adjusted into a date, such as <code>MAKEDATE(2020,4,31) = May 1, 2020</code> rather than returning an error that there is no 31st day of April.</p>
                                        <p>Available for Tableau Data Extracts. Check for availability in other data sources.</p>
                                        <p><code>MAKEDATE</code> requires numerical inputs for the parts of a date. If your data is a string that should be a date, try the <code><a href="#top" class="xref">DATE</a></code> function. <code>DATE</code> automatically recognizes many standard date formats. If <code>DATE</code> does not recognize the input try using <code><a href="#DATEPARS" class="xref">DATEPARSE</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MAKEDATETIME

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">

                                <tr>

                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Datetime</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>

                                </tr>

                                    </td>

                                        <p><code><a href="#MAKETIME" class="xref">MAKETIME</a></code> is a similar function available for Tableau Data Extracts and some other data sources.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL</code> if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MIN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MIN(expression)</code> or <code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the minimum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN </code>can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MIN(4,7) = 4<br>MIN(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #3/25/1986#<br>MIN([Name]) = "Abebi"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN</code> is usually the value that comes first in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MIN</code> string value is lowest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MIN</code> is the earliest date. If <code>MIN</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MIN</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MAX" class="xref">MAX</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>
