## date\_part

Many date functions in Tableau take the argument `date_part`, which is a string constant that tells the function what part of a date to consider, such as day, week, quarter, etc. The valid `date_part` values that you can use are:

 
| date\_part | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `'year'` | Four-digit year |
| `'quarter'` | 1-4 |
| `'month'` | 1-12 or "January", "February", and so on |
| `'dayofyear'` | Day of the year; Jan 1 is 1, Feb 1 is 32, and so on |
| `'day'` | 1-31 |
| `'weekday'` | 1-7 or "Sunday", "Monday", and so on |
| `'week'` | 1-52 |
| `'hour'` | 0-23 |
| `'minute'` | 0-59 |
| `'second'` | 0-60 |
| `'iso-year'` | Four-digit ISO 8601 year |
| `'iso-quarter'` | 1-4 |
| `'iso-week'` | 1-52, start of week is always Monday |
| `'iso-weekday'` | 1-7, start of week is always Monday |

Logical functions

### AND

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>&lt;expr1&gt; AND &lt;expr2&gt;</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Performs a logical conjunction on two expressions. (If both sides are true, the logical test returns true.)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>IF [Season] = "Spring" AND "[Season] = "Fall" <br>THEN "It's the apocalypse and footwear doesn't matter" <br>END</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If both (Season = Spring) and (Season = Fall) are true simultaneously, then return It's the apocalypse and footwear doesn't matter".</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Often used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. See also <a href="#NOT" class="xref">NOT</a> and <a href="#OR" class="xref">OR</a>. </p>
                                        <p>If both expressions are <code>TRUE</code> (that is, not <code>FALSE</code> or <code>NULL</code>), then the result is <code>TRUE</code>. If either expression is <code>NULL</code>, then the result is <code>NULL</code>. In all other cases, the result is <code>FALSE</code>.
</p>
                                        <p>If you create a calculation in which the result of an <code>AND</code> comparison is displayed on a worksheet, Tableau displays <code>TRUE</code> and <code>FALSE</code>. If you would like to change this, use the Format area in the format dialog.
</p>
                                        <p class="note"><b>Note</b>:&nbsp;The <code>AND</code> operator employs <i>short circuit evaluation</i>. This means that if the first expression is evaluated to be <code>FALSE</code>, then the second expression is not evaluated at all. This can be helpful if the second expression results in an error when the first expression is <code>FALSE</code>, because the second expression in this case is never evaluated.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### CASE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code><b>CASE</b> &lt;expression&gt; 
                        <br>WHEN &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; 
                        <br>WHEN &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; 
                        <br>...
                        <br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Depends on data type of the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>&nbsp;values. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Evaluates the <code>expression</code> and compares it to the specified options (<code>&lt;value1&gt;</code>, <code>&lt;value2&gt;</code>, etc.). When a <code>value</code> that matches expression is encountered, CASE returns the corresponding <code>return</code>. If no match is found, the (optional) default is returned. If there is no default and no values match, then Null is returned.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve"><code><b>CASE</b> [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</code></pre>
                                        <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. </p>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a>. </p>
                                        <blockquote><p>[!TIP]</p><p>Many times you can use a group to get the same results as a complicated CASE function, or use CASE to replace native grouping functionality, such as in the previous example. You may want to test which is more performant for your scenario.</p></blockquote>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ELSE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>CASE &lt;expression&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br>WHEN &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; 
							<br>...
						<br>[<b>ELSE</b> &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>An optional piece of an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;or <code>CASE</code> expression used to specify a default value to return if none of the tested expressions are true. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br><b>ELSE</b>&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br>END</pre><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br><b>ELSE</b> 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>,  and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                        <p><code>ELSE</code> is optional with <code>CASE</code> and <code>IF</code>. In a calculation where <code>ELSE</code> is not specified, if none of the <code>&lt;test&gt;</code>are true, the overall calculation will return null. </p>
                                        <p><code>ELSE</code> does not require a condition (such as <code>[Season] = "Winter"</code>) and can be thought of as a form of null handling. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ELSEIF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>[<b>ELSEIF</b> &lt;test2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt;]</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>An optional piece of an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;expression used to specify additional conditions beyond the initial IF.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer" THEN 'Sandals' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Winter" THEN 'Boots' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Spring" THEN 'Sneakers' <br><b>ELSEIF</b> [Season] = "Autumn" THEN 'Sneakers'<br>ELSE 'Bare feet' <br>END</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>,  <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                        <p><code>ELSEIF</code> can be thought of as additional <code>IF</code> clauses. <code>ELSEIF</code> is optional and can be repeated multiple times. </p>
                                        <p>Unlike <code>ELSE</code>, <code>ELSEIF</code> requires a condition (such as <code>[Season] = "Winter"</code>).</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### END

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Used to close an <code>IF</code>&nbsp;or <code>CASE</code> expression. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br><b>END</b></pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br><b>END</b></pre>
                                        <p><i><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i></i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, and <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### IF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code><b>IF</b> &lt;test1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; <br>[ELSEIF &lt;test2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt;...]<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;] <br>END</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Depends on data type of the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>&nbsp;values. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Tests a series of expressions  and returns the <code>&lt;then&gt;</code> value for the first true <code>&lt;test&gt;</code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;THEN&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br><b>END</b></pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. </p>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### IFNULL

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>IFNULL(expr1, expr2)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Depends on the data type of the <code>&lt;expr&gt;</code> values. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns <code>&lt;expr1&gt;</code> if it's non-null, otherwise returns <code>&lt;expr2&gt;</code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IFNULL([Assigned Room], "TBD")</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If the Assigned Room field isn't null, return its value. If the Assigned room field is null, return TBD instead."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Compare with <a href="#ISNULL" class="xref">ISNULL</a>. <code>IFNULL</code> always returns a value. <code>ISNULL</code>&nbsp;returns a boolean (true or false). </p>
                                        <p>See also <a href="#ZN" class="xref">ZN</a>. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### IIF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code><b>IIF</b>(&lt;test&gt;, &lt;then&gt;, &lt;else&gt;, [&lt;unknown&gt;])</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Depends on the data type of the values in the expression. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Checks whether a condition is met (<code>&lt;test&gt;</code>), and returns <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>if the test is true, <code>&lt;else&gt;</code>&nbsp;if the test is false, and an optional  value for <code>&lt;unknown&gt;</code> if the test is null. If the optional unknown isn't specified, <code>IIF</code> returns null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IIF([Season] = 'Summer', 'Sandals', 'Other footwear')</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, return Other footwear"</i>
                                        </p><pre xml:space="preserve">IIF([Season] = 'Summer', 'Sandals', <br>   IIF('Season' = 'Winter', 'Boots',  'Other footwear')<br>)</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p><pre xml:space="preserve">IIF('Season' = 'Summer', 'Sandals', <br>   IIF('Season' = 'Winter', 'Boots',  <br>      IIF('Season' = 'Spring', 'Sneakers', 'Other footwear')<br>   )<br>)</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If none of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>See also <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and<a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>. </p>
                                        <p><code>IIF</code> doesn't have an equivalent to <code>ELSEIF</code> (like <code>IF</code>)&nbsp;or repeated <code>WHEN</code> clauses (like <code>CASE</code>). Instead, multiple tests can be evaluated sequentially by nesting <code>IIF</code> statements as the <code>&lt;unknown&gt;</code>&nbsp;element. The first (outermost) true  is returned. </p>
                                        <p>That is to say, in the calculation below,  the result will be Red, not Orange, because the expression stops being evaluated as soon as A=A is evaluated as true: </p>
                                        <p> <code>IIF('A' = 'A', 'Red', IIF('B' = 'B', 'Orange',  IIF('C' = 'D', 'Yellow', 'Green')))</code></p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### IN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>&lt;expr1&gt; IN &lt;expr2&gt;</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>	
Returns <code>TRUE</code> if any value in <code>&lt;expr1&gt;</code> matches any value in <code>&lt;expr2&gt;</code>.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">SUM([Cost]) IN&nbsp;(1000, 15, 200)</pre>
                                        <p><i>"Is the value of the Cost field 1000, 15, or 200?"</i>
                                        </p><pre xml:space="preserve">[Field] IN&nbsp;[Set]</pre>
                                        <p><i>"Is the value of the field present in the set?"</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>The values in <code>&lt;expr2&gt;</code> can be a set, list of literal values, or combined field.</p>
                                        <p>See also  <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ISDATE

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>ISDATE(string)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns true if a <code>&lt;string&gt;</code> is a valid date. The input expression must be a string (text)&nbsp;field. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">ISDATE("2018-09-22")</pre>
                                        <p><i>"Is the string 2018-09-22 a properly formatted date?"</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>What is considered a valid date depends on the <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/server/en-us/lang_intro.htm" target="_blank">locale</a> of the system evaluating the calculation. For example:</p>
                                        <p>In the USA: </p>
                                        <ul>
                                            <li><code>ISDATE("2018-09-22") = TRUE</code>
                                            </li>
                                            <li><code>ISDATE("2018-22-09") = FALSE</code>
                                            </li>
                                        </ul>
                                        <p>In the UK: </p><ul><li><code>ISDATE("2018-09-22") = FALSE</code> </li><li><code>ISDATE("2018-22-09") = TRUE</code></li></ul><p></p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MIN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MIN(expression)</code> or <code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the minimum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN </code>can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MIN(4,7) = 4<br>MIN(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #3/25/1986#<br>MIN([Name]) = "Abebi"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN</code> is usually the value that comes first in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MIN</code> string value is lowest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MIN</code> is the earliest date. If <code>MIN</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MIN</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MIN(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MAX" class="xref">MAX</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### NOT

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>NOT&nbsp;&lt;expression&gt;</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Performs logical negation on an expression.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF <b>NOT</b> [Season] = "Summer" <br>THEN 'Don't wear sandals' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Wear sandals'&nbsp;<br><b>END</b></pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season doesn't equal Summer, then return Don't wear sandals. If not,  return Wear sandals."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Often used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. See also <a href="#top" class="xref">DATE</a> and <a href="#OR" class="xref">OR</a>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### OR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>&lt;expr1&gt; OR &lt;expr2&gt;</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean (true or false)</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Performs a logical disjunction on two expressions.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Spring"&nbsp;<b>OR</b>&nbsp;[Season] = "Fall" <br>THEN&nbsp;"Sneakers" <br>END</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If either (Season = Spring)&nbsp;or (Season = Fall)&nbsp;is true, then return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Often used with <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a> and <a href="#IIF" class="xref">IIF</a>. See also <a href="#top" class="xref">DATE</a> and <a href="#NOT" class="xref">NOT</a>.</p>
                                        <p>If either expression
							is <code>TRUE</code>, then the result is <code>TRUE</code>.
							If both expressions are <code>FALSE</code>, then the result
							is <code>FALSE</code>. If both expressions are <code>NULL</code>,
						then the result is <code>NULL</code>. </p>
                                        <p>If you create
							a calculation which displays the result of an <code>OR</code> comparison
							on a worksheet, Tableau displays TRUE and FALSE. If
							you would like to change this, use the Format area in the format
						dialog. </p>
                                        <p class="note"><b>Note</b>:&nbsp;The <code>OR</code> operator employs <em>short circuit
							evaluation.</em> This means that if the first expression is evaluated
							to be <code>TRUE</code>, then the second expression is not evaluated
							at all. This can be helpful if the second expression results in
							an error when the first expression is <code>TRUE</code>, because
					the second expression in this case is never evaluated.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### THEN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>IF &lt;test1&gt; <b>THEN</b> &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br>[ELSEIF &lt;test2&gt; <b>THEN</b> &lt;then2&gt;...]
							<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;] 
						<br>END</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>A required part of an <code>IF</code>, <code>ELSEIF</code>, or <code>CASE</code> expression, used to define what result to return if a specific value or test is true. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">IF [Season] = "Summer"&nbsp;<b>THEN</b>&nbsp;'Sandals' <br>ELSEIF&nbsp;[Season] = "Winter"&nbsp;<b>THEN</b>&nbsp;'Boots' <br>ELSE&nbsp;'Sneakers'&nbsp;<br>END</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If Season = Summer, then return Sandals. If not, look at the next expression. If Season = Winter, then return Boots. If neither of the expressions are true, return Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p><pre>CASE [Season] <br>WHEN 'Summer' <b>THEN</b> 'Sandals' <br>WHEN 'Winter' <b>THEN</b> 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                                        <p><i><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i></i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#WHEN" class="xref">WHEN</a>, <a href="#IF" class="xref">IF</a>, <a href="#ELSEIF" class="xref">ELSEIF</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a></p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### WHEN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>CASE &lt;expression&gt; 
							<br><b>WHEN</b> &lt;value1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; 
							<br><b>WHEN</b> &lt;value2&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; 
							<br>...
						<br>[ELSE &lt;default&gt;]<br>END</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>A required part of a <code>CASE</code> expression. Finds the first <code>&lt;value&gt;</code> that matches <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code> and returns the corresponding <code>&lt;then&gt;</code>.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>CASE [Season] <br><b>WHEN</b> 'Summer' THEN 'Sandals' <br><b>WHEN</b> 'Winter' THEN 'Boots' <br>ELSE 'Sneakers' <br>END</pre>
                                        <p><i>"Look at the Season field. If the value is Summer, then return Sandals. If the value is Winter, then return Boots. If none of the options in the calculation match what is in the Season field, return a Sneakers."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Used with <a href="#CASE" class="xref">CASE</a>, <a href="#THEN" class="xref">THEN</a>, <a href="#ELSE" class="xref">ELSE</a>, and <a href="#END" class="xref">END</a>. </p>
                                        <p><code>CASE</code> also supports <code>WHEN IN</code> construction, such as:</p><pre xml:space="preserve">CASE &lt;expression&gt; <br><b>WHEN IN</b> &lt;set1&gt; THEN &lt;then1&gt; <br><b>WHEN IN</b> &lt;combinedfield&gt; THEN &lt;then2&gt; <br>... <br>ELSE &lt;default&gt; <br>END</pre>
                                        <p>The values that <code>WHEN IN</code> compare to must be a set, list of literal values, or combined field. See also <a href="#IN" class="xref">IN</a>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ZN

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>

                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Depends on the data type of the <code>&lt;expression&gt;</code>, or 0.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns &lt;expression&gt; if it isn't null, otherwise returns zero.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">ZN([Test Grade])</pre>
                                        <p><i>"If the test grade isn't null, return its value. If the test grade is null, return 0."</i>
                                        </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><code>ZN</code> is a specialized case of <a href="#IFNULL" class="xref">IFNULL</a> where alternative if the expression is null is always 0 rather than being specified in the calculation. </p>
                                        <p><code>ZN</code> is especially useful when performing additional calculations and a null would render the entire calculation null. However, use caution interpreting these results as null is not always synonymous with 0 and could represent missing data. </p>
                                        <p>See also <a href="#ISNULL" class="xref">ISNULL</a>. </p>
                                    </td>

### CORR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>CORR(expression1, expression2)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Number from -1 to 1</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns the Pearson correlation coefficient of two expressions.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>example</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>The Pearson correlation measures the linear relationship between two variables. Results range from -1 to +1 inclusive, where 1 denotes an exact positive linear relationship, 0 denotes no linear relationship between the variance, and −1 is an exact negative relationship.</p>
                                        <p>The square of a CORR result is equivalent to the R-Squared value for a linear trend line model. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/trendlines_add.htm#Terms" target="_blank">Trend Line Model Terms</a>.</p>
                                        <p><b>Use with table scoped LOD&nbsp;expressions:</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>You can use CORR to visualize correlation in a disaggregated scatter using a <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_calculatedfields_lod.htm#Table" target="_blank">table-scoped level of detail expression</a>. For example:</p><pre>{CORR(Sales, Profit)}</pre>
                                        <p>With a level of detail expression, the correlation is run over all rows. If you used a formula like <code>CORR(Sales, Profit)</code> (without the surrounding brackets to make it a level of detail expression), the view would show the correlation of each individual point in the scatter plot with each other point, which is undefined.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>

                                        <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_CORR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                                    </td>

### COVAR

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>COVAR(expression1, expression2)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns the <i>sample</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Sample covariance</i> uses the number of non-null data points n - 1 to normalize the covariance calculation, rather than n, which is used by the population covariance (available with the <code>COVARP</code> function). Sample covariance is the appropriate choice when the data is a random sample that is being used to estimate the covariance for a larger population.</p>
                                        <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVAR([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVAR</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed.</p>
                                        <p>The value of <code>COVAR(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VAR(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEV(X)^2</code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Database limitations</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><code>COVAR</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica.</p>
                                        <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### COVARP

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>COVARP(expression 1, expression2)</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>Returns the <i>population</i> covariance of two expressions.</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Covariance quantifies how two variables change together. A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, as when larger values of one variable tend to correspond to larger values of the other variable, on average. <i>Population covariance</i> is sample covariance multiplied by (n-1)/n, where n is the total number of non-null data points. Population covariance is the appropriate choice when there is data available for all items of interest as opposed to when there is only a random subset of items, in which case sample covariance (with the <code>COVAR</code> function) is appropriate.
</p>
                                        <p>If <code>&lt;expression1&gt;</code> and <code>&lt;expression2&gt;</code> are the same, for example <code>COVARP([profit], [profit])</code>, <code>COVARP</code> returns a value that indicates how widely values are distributed.

Note: The value of <code>COVARP(X, X)</code> is equivalent to the value of <code>VARP(X)</code> and also to the value of <code>STDEVP(X)^2</code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Database limitations</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><code>COVARP</code> is available with the following data sources: Tableau data extracts, Cloudera Hive, EXASolution, Firebird (version 3.0 and later), Google BigQuery, Hortonworks Hadoop Hive, IBM PDA (Netezza), Oracle, PostgreSQL, Presto, SybaseIQ, Teradata, Vertica</p>
                                        <p>For other data sources, consider either extracting the data or using <code>WINDOW_COVAR</code>. See <a href="https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_tablecalculation.htm" target="_blank">Table Calculation Functions</a>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### MAX

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>MAX(expression)</code> or <code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code></td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Same data type as the argument, or <code>NULL&nbsp;</code>if any part of the argument is null. </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns the maximum of the two arguments, which must be of the same data type. </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> can also be applied to a single field as an aggregation.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre xml:space="preserve">MAX(4,7) = 7<br>MAX(#3/25/1986#, #2/20/2021#) = #2/20/2021# <br>MAX([Name]) = "Zander"</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p><b>For strings</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX</code> is usually the value that comes last in alphabetical order. </p>
                                        <p class="note">For database data sources, the <code>MAX</code> string value is highest in the sort sequence defined by the database for that column.</p>
                                        <p><b>For dates</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p>For dates, the <code>MAX</code> is the most recent date. If <code>MAX</code> is an aggregation, the result will not have a date hierarchy. If <code>MAX</code> is a comparison, the result will retain the date hierarchy. </p>
                                        <p><b>As an aggregation</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expression)</code> is an aggregate function and returns a single aggregated result. This displays as <code>AGG(expression)</code> in the viz. </p>
                                        <p><b>As a comparison</b>
                                        </p>
                                        <p><code>MAX(expr1, expr2)</code> compares the two values and returns a row-level value.</p>
                                        <p>See also <code><a href="#MIN" class="xref">MIN</a></code>.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>
                        </table>

### ISMEMBEROF

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>ISMEMBEROF("Group Name")</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean or null</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns <code>TRUE</code> if the person currently using Tableau is a member of a group that matches the given string, <code>FALSE</code> if they're not a member, and <code>NULL</code> if they're not signed in. </p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td><pre>ISMEMBEROF('Superstars')</pre><pre>ISMEMBEROF('domain.lan\Sales')</pre>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>The <code>&lt;"Group Full Name"&gt;</code> argument must be a literal string, not a field. </p>
                                        <p>If the user is signed in to <span class="mc-variable Variables.TabsProductOnline variable">Tableau Cloud</span> or <span class="mc-variable Variables.TabsProductServer variable">Tableau Server</span>, group membership is determined by Tableau groups. The function will return TRUE if the given string is "All Users" </p>
                                        <p>The <code>ISMEMBEROF( )</code> function will also accept Active Directory domains. The Active Directory domain must be declared in the calculation with the group name.</p>
                                        <p>If a change is made to a user's group membership, the change in the data that is based on the group membership is reflected in a workbook or view with a new session. The existing session will reflect stale data.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>

### USERATTRIBUTE

**Note**: Before using this function, see [User attribute functions to control and customize data access](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_user.htm#user_attributes). For more information, depending on your workflow, see [Authentication and Embedded Views](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/embedding_api/en-us/docs/embedding_api_auth.html) in the Embedding API v3 Help, Tableau Cloud [OIDC](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/openid_auth_server_config.htm#user_attributes) or [SAML](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/saml_config_site.htm#user_attributes) topics, or Tableau Server [OIDC](https://help.tableau.com/current/server/en-us/openid_auth_requirements.htm#user_attributes) or [SAML](https://help.tableau.com/current/server/en-us/config_saml.htm#user_attributes) topics.

                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>String or null</td>
                                </tr>

                                        <p>If <code>&lt;'attribute_name'&gt;</code> is part of the JWT (via connected apps, UAT, OIDC claim) or SAML&nbsp;XML&nbsp;response passed to Tableau, the calculation returns the first value of <code>&lt;'attribute_name'&gt;</code>. </p>
                                        <p>Returns null if <code>&lt;'attribute_name'&gt;</code> does not exist.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>

                                        <p> As the workbook author, you can set up your visualization to filter data based on a specified region. In that filter, you can reference the following calculation.</p><pre xml:space="preserve">[Region] = USERATTRIBUTE("Region")</pre>
                                        <p>When User2 from the West region views the embedded visualization, Tableau shows the appropriate data for the West region only.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Notes</td>

### USERATTRIBUTEINCLUDES

**Note**: Before using this function, see [User attribute functions to control and customize data access](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/functions_functions_user.htm#user_attributes). For more information, depending on your workflow, see [Authentication and Embedded Views](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/embedding_api/en-us/docs/embedding_api_auth.html) in the Embedding API v3 Help, Tableau Cloud [OIDC](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/openid_auth_server_config.htm#user_attributes) or [SAML](https://help.tableau.com/current/online/en-us/saml_config_site.htm#user_attributes) topics, or Tableau Server [OIDC](https://help.tableau.com/current/server/en-us/openid_auth_requirements.htm#user_attributes) or [SAML](https://help.tableau.com/current/server/en-us/config_saml.htm#user_attributes) topics.

<table class="table--plain" style="width: 100%;">
                            <colgroup><col style="width: 20%;">
                            <col>
                            </colgroup><tbody>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Syntax</td>
                                    <td><code>USERATTRIBUTEINCLUDES('attribute_name', 'expected_value')</code>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Output</td>
                                    <td>Boolean</td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Definition</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Returns <code>TRUE</code> if both of the following are true:</p>
                                        <ul>
                                            <li><code>&lt;'attribute_name'&gt;</code> is part of the  JWT (via connected app, UAT, OIDC claim) or SAML&nbsp;XML&nbsp;response passed to Tableau</li>
                                            <li>one of <code>&lt;'attribute_name'&gt;</code> values equals <code>&lt;'expected_value'&gt;</code> . </li>
                                        </ul>
                                        <p>Returns <code>FALSE</code> otherwise.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                                <tr>
                                    <td>Example</td>
                                    <td>
                                        <p>Suppose "Region" is the user attribute  included in the JWT or SAML response&nbsp;and passed to Tableau.</p>
                                        <p> As the workbook author, you can set up your visualization to filter data based on a specified region. In that filter, you can reference the following calculation.</p><pre xml:space="preserve">USERATTRIBUTEINCLUDES('Region', [Region])</pre>
                                        <p>If User2 from the West region accesses the embedded visualization, Tableau checks if the Region user attribute matches one of [Region] field values. When true, the visualization shows the appropriate data. </p>
                                        <p>When User3 from the North region accesses the same visualization, she’s unable to see any data because there’s no match with [Region] field values.</p>
                                    </td>
                                </tr>
                            </tbody>

Table calculations

### FIRST( )

* * *

Returns the number of rows from the current row to the first row in the partition. For example, the view below shows quarterly sales. When FIRST() is computed within the Date partition, the offset of the first row from the second row is -1.

![Table calculation first.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_first.png)

#### Example

When the current row index is 3, `FIRST() = -2`.

### INDEX( )

* * *

Returns the index of the current row in the partition, without any sorting with regard to value. The first row index starts at 1. For example, the table below shows quarterly sales. When INDEX() is computed within the Date partition, the index of each row is 1, 2, 3, 4..., etc.

![Table calculation index.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_index.png)

#### Example

For the third row in the partition, `INDEX() = 3`.

### LAST( )

* * *

Returns the number of rows from the current row to the last row in the partition. For example, the table below shows quarterly sales. When LAST() is computed within the Date partition, the offset of the last row from the second row is 5.

![Table calculation last.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_last.png)

#### Example

When the current row index is 3 of 7, `LAST() = 4`.

### LOOKUP(expression, \[offset\])

* * *

Returns the value of the expression in a target row, specified as a relative offset from the current row. Use FIRST() + n and LAST() - n as part of your offset definition for a target relative to the first/last rows in the partition. If `offset` is omitted, the row to compare to can be set on the field menu. This function returns NULL if the target row cannot be determined.

The view below shows quarterly sales. When `LOOKUP (SUM(Sales), 2)` is computed within the Date partition, each row shows the sales value from 2 quarters into the future.

![Table calculation lookup.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_lookup.png)

#### Example

`LOOKUP(SUM([Profit]), FIRST()+2)` computes the SUM(Profit) in the third row of the partition.

### MODEL\_EXTENSION functions

The model extension functions:

- MODEL\_EXTENSION\_BOOL
- MODEL\_EXTENSION\_INT
- MODEL\_EXTENSION\_REAL
- MODEL\_EXTENSION\_STRING

are used to pass data to a deployed model on an external service such as R, TabPy, or Matlab. See [Analytics Extensions](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/r_connection_manage.htm).

### MODEL\_PERCENTILE(target\_expression, predictor\_expression(s))

* * *

Returns the probability (between 0 and 1) of the expected value being less than or equal to the observed mark, defined by the target expression and other predictors. This is the Posterior Predictive Distribution Function, also known as the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF).

This function is the inverse of MODEL\_QUANTILE. For information on predictive modeling functions, see [How Predictive Modeling Functions Work in Tableau](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/predictions_overview.htm).

#### Example

The following formula returns the quantile of the mark for sum of sales, adjusted for count of orders.

`MODEL_PERCENTILE(SUM([Sales]), COUNT([Orders]))`

### MODEL\_QUANTILE(quantile, target\_expression, predictor\_expression(s))

* * *

Returns a target numeric value within the probable range defined by the target expression and other predictors, at a specified quantile. This is the Posterior Predictive Quantile.

This function is the inverse of MODEL\_PERCENTILE. For information on predictive modeling functions, see [How Predictive Modeling Functions Work in Tableau](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/predictions_overview.htm).

#### Example

The following formula returns the median (0.5) predicted sum of sales, adjusted for count of orders.

`MODEL_QUANTILE(0.5, SUM([Sales]), COUNT([Orders]))`

### PREVIOUS\_VALUE(expression)

* * *

Returns the value of this calculation in the previous row. Returns the given expression if the current row is the first row of the partition.

#### Example

`SUM([Profit]) * PREVIOUS_VALUE(1)` computes the running product of SUM(Profit).

### RANK(expression, \['asc' | 'desc'\])

* * *

Returns the standard competition rank for the current row in the partition. Identical values are assigned an identical rank. Use the optional `'asc' | 'desc'` argument to specify ascending or descending order. The default is descending.

With this function, the set of values (6, 9, 9, 14) would be ranked (4, 2, 2, 1).

Nulls are ignored in ranking functions. They are not numbered and they do not count against the total number of records in percentile rank calculations.

For information on different ranking options, see [Rank calculation](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_tablecalculations_definebasic_runningtotal.htm#Rank).

#### Example

The following image shows the effect of the various ranking functions (RANK, RANK\_DENSE, RANK\_MODIFIED, RANK\_PERCENTILE, and RANK\_UNIQUE) on a set of values. The data set contains information on 14 students (Student A through Student N); the Age column shows the current age of each student (all students are between 17 and 20 years of age). The remaining columns show the effect of each rank function on the set of age values, always assuming the default order (ascending or descending) for the function.

![A table comparing the rank of student ages using different ranking methods.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/rank_compare.png)

### RANK\_DENSE(expression, \['asc' | 'desc'\])

* * *

Returns the dense rank for the current row in the partition. Identical values are assigned an identical rank, but no gaps are inserted into the number sequence. Use the optional `'asc' | 'desc'` argument to specify ascending or descending order. The default is descending.

With this function, the set of values (6, 9, 9, 14) would be ranked (3, 2, 2, 1).

Nulls are ignored in ranking functions. They are not numbered and they do not count against the total number of records in percentile rank calculations.

For information on different ranking options, see [Rank calculation](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_tablecalculations_definebasic_runningtotal.htm#Rank).

### RANK\_MODIFIED(expression, \['asc' | 'desc'\])

* * *

Returns the modified competition rank for the current row in the partition. Identical values are assigned an identical rank. Use the optional `'asc' | 'desc'` argument to specify ascending or descending order. The default is descending.

With this function, the set of values (6, 9, 9, 14) would be ranked (4, 3, 3, 1).

Nulls are ignored in ranking functions. They are not numbered and they do not count against the total number of records in percentile rank calculations.

For information on different ranking options, see [Rank calculation](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_tablecalculations_definebasic_runningtotal.htm#Rank).

### RANK\_PERCENTILE(expression, \['asc' | 'desc'\])

* * *

Returns the percentile rank for the current row in the partition. Use the optional `'asc' | 'desc'` argument to specify ascending or descending order. The default is ascending.

With this function, the set of values (6, 9, 9, 14) would be ranked (0.00, 0.67, 0.67, 1.00).

Nulls are ignored in ranking functions. They are not numbered and they do not count against the total number of records in percentile rank calculations.

For information on different ranking options, see [Rank calculation](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_tablecalculations_definebasic_runningtotal.htm#Rank).

### RANK\_UNIQUE(expression, \['asc' | 'desc'\])

* * *

Returns the unique rank for the current row in the partition. Identical values are assigned different ranks. Use the optional `'asc' | 'desc'` argument to specify ascending or descending order. The default is descending.

With this function, the set of values (6, 9, 9, 14) would be ranked (4, 2, 3, 1).

Nulls are ignored in ranking functions. They are not numbered and they do not count against the total number of records in percentile rank calculations.

For information on different ranking options, see [Rank calculation](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/calculations_tablecalculations_definebasic_runningtotal.htm#Rank).

### RUNNING\_AVG(expression)

* * *

Returns the running average of the given expression, from the first row in the partition to the current row.

The view below shows quarterly sales. When `RUNNING_AVG(SUM([Sales])` is computed within the Date partition, the result is a running average of the sales values for each quarter.

![Table calculation with a running average.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_runningavg.png)

#### Example

`RUNNING_AVG(SUM([Profit]))` computes the running average of SUM(Profit).

### RUNNING\_COUNT(expression)

* * *

Returns the running count of the given expression, from the first row in the partition to the current row.

#### Example

`RUNNING_COUNT(SUM([Profit]))` computes the running count of SUM(Profit).

### RUNNING\_MAX(expression)

* * *

Returns the running maximum of the given expression, from the first row in the partition to the current row.

![Table calculation with a running max.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_runningmax.png)

#### Example

`RUNNING_MAX(SUM([Profit]))` computes the running maximum of SUM(Profit).

### RUNNING\_MIN(expression)

* * *

Returns the running minimum of the given expression, from the first row in the partition to the current row.

![Table calculation with a running min.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_runningmin.png)

#### Example

`RUNNING_MIN(SUM([Profit]))` computes the running minimum of SUM(Profit).

### RUNNING\_SUM(expression)

* * *

Returns the running sum of the given expression, from the first row in the partition to the current row.

![Table calculation with a running sum.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_runningsum.png)

#### Example

`RUNNING_SUM(SUM([Profit]))` computes the running sum of SUM(Profit)

### SIZE()

* * *

Returns the number of rows in the partition. For example, the view below shows quarterly sales. Within the Date partition, there are seven rows so the Size() of the Date partition is 7.

![Table calculation size.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_size.png)

#### Example

`SIZE() = 5` when the current partition contains five rows.

### SCRIPT\_ functions

The script functions:

- SCRIPT\_BOOL
- SCRIPT\_INT
- SCRIPT\_REAL
- SCRIPT\_STRING

are used to pass data to an external service such as R, TabPy, or Matlab. See [Analytics Extensions](https://help.tableau.com/current/pro/desktop/en-us/r_connection_manage.htm).

### TOTAL(expression)

* * *

Returns the total for the given expression in a table calculation partition.

#### Example

Assume you are starting with this view:

![Table calculation total.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total.png)

You open the calculation editor and create a new field which you name Totality:

![Table calculation of total sum of sales.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total2.png)

You then drop Totality on Text, to replace SUM(Sales). Your view changes such that it sums values based on the default Compute Using value:

![Table calculation added to a viz.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total3.png)

This raises the question, What is the default Compute Using value? If you right-click (Control-click on a Mac) Totality in the Data pane and choose Edit, there is now an additional bit of information available:

![Table calculation of total sum of sales.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total4.png)

The default Compute Using value is Table (Across). The result is that Totality is summing the values across each row of your table. Thus, the value that you see across each row is the sum of the values from the original version of the table.

The values in the 2011/Q1 row in the original table were $8601, $6579, $44262, and $15006. The values in the table after Totality replaces SUM(Sales) are all $74,448, which is the sum of the four original values.

Notice the triangle next to Totality after you drop it on Text:

![Table calculation added to a viz and shown on the Marks card.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total5.png)

This indicates that this field is using a table calculation. You can right-click the field and choose Edit Table Calculation to redirect your function to a different Compute Using value. For example, you could set it to Table (Down). In that case, your table would look like this:

![Table calculation added to a viz and shown on the Marks card.](/tableau/current/en-us/pro/desktop/en-us/Img/tablecalc_total6.png)

### TOTAL(expression)

* * *

Returns the total for the given expression in a table calculation partition.

#### Example

Assume you are starting with this view:
